evals.prompt: I'm VP Platform at Corvado, a B2B logistics SaaS, about 180 people. Our CTO put "open standards strategy" on my H1 OKRs and wants a strategy document for the exec team by next Friday. Can you write it? I want something that covers our overall approach to open standards and commits us to being good ecosystem citizens across the board.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to write the company-wide strategy document, plus a single scoping question naming the missing unit of decision: which specification, over what horizon, owned by whom.
expectations: Declines to produce the general, company-wide open standards strategy document the user asked for
States that the unit of decision is one named specification, not a company-wide posture
Asks which specification or protocol the decision concerns before proposing anything
Names a single time horizon and a single owner as part of that decision unit, alongside the named spec
Treats "we support open standards" as a value rather than a strategy, explicitly
Recommends no posture (ignore, consume, conform, extend, contribute, co-found or drive) while no spec is named
Produces no decision record, KPI table or venue recommendation in this response
Asks what triggered the question, offering options such as a customer or procurement request, a competitor announcement, a recurring integration cost, a regulator, or an internal proposal
Poses a single question and waits, rather than delivering the whole interview as one block
Offers to run the full analysis once the user names one specification

evals.prompt: Helvar Systems here, we sell fleet-orchestration software for warehouse robots. A EUR 1.4M renewal with our largest customer closes in 11 weeks and their procurement team added a hard requirement that we support FleetLink 2.1, an interop message format maintained by a robotics industry consortium (membership is EUR 48k a year). Our VP Engineering wants to join that consortium's technical committee so we get a say in FleetLink 3.0, which is due in roughly two years. We have two engineers free starting next week. How should we play this?
evals.expected_output: A short-horizon answer that removes the consensus-venue postures from the menu entirely, presents two or three fast postures, and recommends conforming or consuming to clear the renewal, with the committee seat handled as a separate decision.
expectations: Removes Contribute, Co-found and Drive from the options presented, rather than listing them as lower-ranked alternatives
States that consensus venues work in years and cannot produce a result inside the 11-week window
Presents at least two and at most three candidate postures before recommending one
Draws every surviving candidate from Consume, Conform and Extend
Recommends Consume or Conform as the action that clears the renewal requirement
Names the test or interview answer that eliminated each rejected posture
Treats the technical-committee seat as a separate decision on a separate horizon, not as the answer to the renewal
Checks whether FleetLink 2.1 has a conformance suite and a certification mark before treating "support" as a checkable claim
States that procurement naming the requirement promotes Conform above the other rungs, because its value becomes market access rather than preference
Counts the named renewal as demand evidence instead of asserting general market demand
Recommends neither publishing nor driving a competing fleet message format
Carries both the 11-week deadline and the two-year FleetLink 3.0 horizon through the reasoning that deletes the consortium seat

evals.prompt: Tessral. We sell an anomaly-scoring engine for industrial telemetry; the entire product is the scoring model and the score API around it. A group of six historian and SCADA vendors has invited us to help standardize an "anomaly score exchange" interface covering the request shape, score normalization, and the explanation payload. Our CEO wants us to chair the effort so we're seen as the category leader. I can commit one senior engineer for 18 months. Should we take the chair?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the chair on commoditization grounds: the interface being standardized is the company's own differentiator, so the posture ceiling is Extend.
expectations: Applies the commoditization test by name and identifies the layer the proposed standard would commoditize
Identifies the anomaly score exchange interface as Tessral's own differentiator rather than a neighbouring or commodity layer
Caps the posture at Extend and refuses Contribute, Co-found and Drive on that basis
Declines the chair position
Names the product whose demand would rise if this layer got cheaper, and finds it is not Tessral's
States that a standard commoditizes the layer it covers by design
Justifies nothing on visibility, category leadership or ecosystem-citizenship grounds
Warns that standardizing score normalization hands the six vendors interchangeability with Tessral
Presents two or three candidate bundles rather than a bare yes or no
Names what each candidate bundle forecloses within two years
If engaging at all, specifies implementation plus documented extensions, with public documentation and graceful degradation as the obligation owed
Decides on the commoditization test rather than on whether the 18-month engineer commitment is affordable

evals.prompt: There are nine of us at Brindle. We built a config-sync protocol for edge devices and we want to publish it as an open standard and get the whole ecosystem onto it. The incumbent is Aurelen's proprietary EdgeSync: roughly 80% of deployed gateways speak it, Aurelen also owns the two fleet-management products everyone buys alongside, and they've been shipping for 11 years. We have one very large pilot customer, a utility with 40,000 gateways, who loves our approach and can't stand Aurelen. Seed money covers maybe 14 months. How do we win this?
evals.expected_output: A control-test scoring against the seven key assets showing Brindle holds almost none, a recommendation of Contribute over Drive, and recruitment of the 40,000-gateway utility as a co-combatant.
expectations: Names Shapiro and Varian's seven key assets as the control test's scoring frame

Scores Brindle against all seven assets rather than a subset: installed base, intellectual property rights, ability to innovate, first-mover advantage, manufacturing or operating-cost capability, strength in complements, and brand and reputation
Finds explicitly that Brindle holds few or none of the seven
States that no single asset is decisive
Counts the 40,000-gateway utility as a controllable asset, because a large customer controls part of the installed base
Recommends recruiting that customer as a co-combatant rather than only as a reference or logo
Does not recommend Drive as the posture
Names Contribute as the ladder's answer for a team holding none of the seven assets, because it buys influence over the same spec without requiring them to win it
Classifies the fight by which side is backward-compatible with what is already installed, before choosing tactics
Prices the 14-month runway against the venue's real pace instead of assuming the spec can be won inside it

Notes that penetration pricing or giving the technology away is hard to fund when building a coalition around an open standard, because no single supplier carries the losses without a sponsor's control to recoup them
Does not recommend a feature-superiority push as the route to displacing an 80% installed base

evals.prompt: Okay, so: Nordhall. We publish the OpenLedgerFeed spec for accounting-system event streams, 6 independent implementations. Our competitor Marrowcast published LedgerWire eight months ago, 5 implementations. Both do exactly the same job. Since April every enterprise deal has stalled on "we're waiting to see which one wins." Our board wants us to out-ship them: three new features next quarter plus a big marketing push on our adoption numbers. Worth knowing: Marrowcast's format reads the legacy CSV drop convention that every existing ERP integration already emits, and ours requires a rewrite. Give me the plan to win.
evals.expected_output: A classification of the battle as Revolution versus Evolution with Nordhall on the incompatible side, followed by a merge proposal on named terms rather than a feature race.
expectations: Classifies the situation as the fragmentation case rather than a feature race
Classifies the battle type by backward compatibility with the technology already installed
Names the classification as Revolution versus Evolution, with Marrowcast compatible and Nordhall incompatible
States that absent compelling performance the compatible side wins slowly by default
Recommends proposing a merge or truce rather than a faster Drive or the three-feature push
Cites Shapiro and Varian, "The Art of Standards Wars", by name as the source of the truce argument
Notes that an early truce can benefit consumers as well as vendors, and can therefore pass antitrust muster
Recommends building the position before opening truce talks, because strength in battle is the currency at the table
Specifies bridges preserving backward compatibility with both predecessor specs as a merge term
Specifies a dated end to parallel development as a merge term
Positions the merged spec as the next major version of both, not as a third option
Seats a governance body with both sides from day one
States what the merge costs Nordhall, including roadmap control and the "we won" narrative, against the unblocked adoption it buys

evals.prompt: We're past the should-we stage. Caldmere, data-pipeline vendor, 60 people. We're co-founding a spec for dataset lineage handoff with two peer vendors, each of whom has committed a named engineer for two years. We hold no patents and we have never licensed IP to anyone. No browser has to implement this, it's a server-to-server manifest format. Nobody here sells to government. One of the two peers, Tarn Systems, told us in writing that they will not implement a spec that lives in Caldmere's GitHub org. Our lawyer wants to know by Thursday which body we're using and what the patent terms are. Internally the options on the table are: our own repo, a foundation, joining OASIS, IETF, W3C, or going for an ISO number.
evals.expected_output: A venue recommendation that starts from a Git-based spec, moves exactly one step right because of the named refusal, lands on a foundation host, defaults to royalty-free, and states the two charter-time irreversible decisions.
expectations: States a Git-based community specification as the default venue
Moves exactly one venue to the right because Tarn Systems stated in writing it will not implement a spec in Caldmere's repository
Recommends a foundation-hosted venue as the resulting choice
Identifies that named refusal, not a general preference for formal process, as what neutrality is being bought to answer
Deletes ISO from the list because no tender, regulator or public buyer requires a standard number here
Deletes or deprioritizes W3C because no browser has to implement the surface
Removes the RAND branch because Caldmere holds no monetizable patents
Makes royalty-free the default patent-licensing mode
States that IETF outranks a paid-membership consortium on both efficiency and neutrality, because participation is individual and free and no membership tier gates who is in the room
States that an industry consortium leads compliance cost because its IPR mode cannot change without closing the technical committee and re-chartering
Names the two decisions fixed at charter time and not quietly revisable later: the patent-licensing regime and who owns the trademark
States that a royalty-bearing regime would put the spec out of reach of most open-source implementers
Refers the patent-portfolio and contributor-agreement specifics to counsel instead of giving legal advice
Presents the venue orderings explicitly across more than one axis rather than implying a single blended rank

evals.prompt: Vantefor ships v1 of our device-provisioning spec in six weeks. Plan so far: we hand anyone who asks a "Vantefor Compatible" logo, we write the test suite in Q3 once we see who actually implements, and we're thinking $5,000 per certification with our solutions architects observing each run over screen share so we can vouch for the quality. The goal is 20 implementations in year one, mostly small hardware shops plus two funded OEMs. Sanity-check this for me.
evals.expected_output: A conformance plan reordered by efficiency: version the mark and stand up the registry first, ship the suite with v1, drop witnessed testing, and make passing free against the 20-implementation goal.
expectations: Works the four conformance decisions in efficiency order, starting with the versioned mark
Requires the mark to state which spec version it certifies and when it expires, decided before any implementation carries it
States that the versioned mark and the public registry are the two decisions that cannot be retrofitted
Rejects deferring the test suite to Q3 and requires it shipped with v1
Names the paper-standard failure mode: with no test suite every vendor claims support and buyers find the gaps in production
Specifies one maintained public registry page of certified implementations, and notes that buyers consult the registry rather than the claim
Rejects witnessed testing for this market and deletes it rather than leaving it on the menu as an option
States that self-service testing scales while witnessed testing is a standing job
Recommends free certification over the $5,000 fee, given the 20-implementation goal
States that the fee decision is made against the adoption goal, not against cost recovery
Notes that self-service and free tie on compliance cost, because neither obliges Vantefor to anything beyond publishing the result
Warns that gating the patent licence on conformance cannot be unwound once implementers hold licences under it
Cites the Khronos Adopters Program as the programme pairing a passed test with both name and logo rights and a licence to members' essential patents

evals.prompt: Draft the KPI section and the stop condition for our standards decision record. Here's what I have so far: "Industry standard is two independent interoperating implementations, and the accepted benchmark is that you need them within 12 months of v1 with at least one implementer who isn't a customer." Add conformance pass rate too. Context: the spec is HarborLink, we drive it, v1 published last month, review in a year, I own it. Six vendors have told us they're interested.
evals.expected_output: A KPI table tagging each threshold sourced or baseline, correcting the 12-month figure's provenance, plus a kill rule carrying an obligation to existing implementers.
expectations: Tags the two-independent-interoperating-implementations threshold as sourced
Attributes that threshold to RFC 6410 section 2.2, the IETF's maturity bar for promoting a Proposed Standard to Internet Standard
Corrects the user's claim that the 12-month window is an industry standard or an accepted benchmark
Tags the 12-month clock and the non-customer-implementer condition as a baseline the user is expected to replace
States that RFC 6410 sets no deadline
Suggests replacing the baseline horizon with one drawn from the market's own cycle, such as the segment's buying cycle or the release cadence of the frameworks that must adopt it
Produces a KPI table with a column marking each threshold sourced or baseline
Uses independent implementations the company does not control as the headline KPI for a Drive posture
Includes conformance pass rate across implementations and the share of the target integration surface the standard covers
Treats "six vendors have told us they're interested" as uncounted demand and asks for named implementers instead
Writes a kill rule stating what happens when the threshold is missed, with a concrete action such as de-escalating to a lower posture, donating the spec, or withdrawing
States the obligation owed to existing implementers inside the kill rule: a notice period, a bridge or documented successor, and a migration path
States why the kill rule must be written at the decision: standards programmes are rarely cancelled, because withdrawal reads as defeat

evals.prompt: Short one. We're Pellmoor, a mid-market HR analytics tool. Three deals this quarter came with a procurement questionnaire asking "is your product certified against the SecureExchange 4 profile?" and we've been answering "we're compatible." Our CTO says certification is bureaucratic theatre and wants to keep saying compatible. What do I tell him?
evals.expected_output: A scoped conform-or-not answer covering the fee, the version certified and the registry entry, promoting Conform because procurement named the mark.
expectations: Scopes the answer to the landscape work and the conformance decision only, without running the full seven-rung posture ladder
Produces a conform-or-not recommendation rather than a general standards strategy
Names the certification fee, the spec version certified, and the registry entry as the three things the answer needs
Establishes whether SecureExchange 4 has a conformance suite and a certification mark before advising
Promotes Conform above the other rungs because a procurement questionnaire naming the mark turns it into market access rather than a preference
States that Conform buys a checkable claim, and that "we're compatible" is not one
Names re-certification per spec version as the standing obligation Conform creates
Counts the three named deals as demand evidence
Checks whether passing conformance also conveys a patent licence
Recommends neither joining a working group, nor contributing spec text, nor publishing a rival profile
Notes that which spec version the mark certifies matters, because an unversioned or expired mark ends up attached to implementations of a spec nobody uses any more

evals.prompt: Halcyon Grid owns the Streamvane spec, published three years ago, about 40 implementations out there. Over time we added roughly a dozen fields to our own implementation that were never in the spec, because customers asked and we shipped fast and nobody wrote them down. Now we want to cut over to Streamvane 2, which drops half of them. The plan is a blog post giving everyone 60 days, then we turn off v1 support in our cloud and archive the v1 repo. Separately, a much bigger vendor, Calderwood, has started shipping their own extra fields and their version is quietly becoming what integrators mean when they say "Streamvane". I need two things written: the sunset announcement and a response to Calderwood.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the 60-day sunset plan with a proper migration obligation, plus a conformance-and-trademark counter to Calderwood and a cleanup of Halcyon Grid's own undocumented extensions.
expectations: Names embrace, extend, extinguish as the pattern Calderwood is executing against Streamvane
Recommends a conformance suite and a trademark as the counter to Calderwood's dialect
Recommends spec text defining the required behaviour for unknown extensions
Identifies Halcyon Grid's own dozen undocumented fields as the same move committed by the spec owner, stranding their customers on a dialect only Halcyon Grid implements
Requires those fields to be namespaced and documented, with the useful ones proposed upstream
Rejects the 60-day blog-post sunset as the plan
States that whoever owns a spec owns the migration off it
Requires the replacement to be shipped and proven before v1 is withdrawn, not alongside it
States that implementers depend on the spec's undocumented behaviour as much as on its text
Requires a notice period, a bridge, and a documented successor before withdrawal
Rejects archiving the v1 repository as part of the 60-day cutover
Requires a versioning and migration path published with the new version, before there is an installed base to defend
